text: Sir Martyn Poliakoff, born on 16 December 1947, is a British chemist renowned for his contributions to green chemistry and as the primary presenter on the YouTube channel Periodic Videos. His academic research focuses on supercritical fluids, infrared spectroscopy, and lasers, and he holds the position of research professor in chemistry at the University of Nottingham. He has taught various modules, including green chemistry, and has been involved in research funded by the EPSRC. Poliakoff was born to a British-Jewish mother, Ina (née Montagu), and a Russian-Jewish father, Alexander Poliakoff; he has a younger brother, screenwriter and director Stephen Poliakoff, and his paternal grandfather, Joseph Poliakoff, was an electrical device inventor who emigrated to the United Kingdom in 1924 after experiencing the communist revolution in Russia. He studied chemistry at King's College, Cambridge, earning a BA in 1969 and a PhD in 1973 under J.J. Turner. In 1972, he moved to Newcastle University and was appointed lecturer at the University of Nottingham in 1979, later promoted to professor in 1991. Poliakoff is a global leader in green chemistry, particularly in the use of supercritical fluids, which combine gas and liquid properties to enable chemical reactions without harmful organic solvents, leading to the industrial-scale development of supercritical carbon dioxide and water solvent systems. From 2011 to 2016, he served as foreign secretary and vice-president of the Royal Society, advocating for UK science internationally. He is the narrator of over 600 short videos in The Periodic Table of Videos, a science project by Brady Haran initially aimed at introducing the public to the 118 elements, which has since expanded to include molecules and other chemical topics. He gained public attention for calculating that the FIFA World Cup Trophy could not be made of solid gold due to its excessive weight. Poliakoff presented videos at IUPAC's elements inauguration in Moscow. In 2019, he collaborated with his daughter Ellen Poliakoff to create an upside-down periodic table to aid young learners. He received the Meldola Medal and Prize in 1976, was elected Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) and Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry (FRSC) in 2002, and Fellow of the Institution of Chemical Engineers (FIChemE) in 2004, serving on the IChemE Council from 2009 to 2013. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2008 New Year Honours and has been a member of the Advisory Council for the Campaign for Science and Engineering since 2008. In 2008, he was elected an Honorary Member of the Chemical Society of Ethiopia and a Foreign Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 2011. In 2011, he won the Nyholm Prize for Education. He received an Honorary Doctorate from Heriot-Watt University in 2011. In 2012, he was elected a Fellow of the Academia Europaea and in 2013, an Associate Fellow of TWAS. In 2014, he became an Associate Member of the Ethiopian Academy of Sciences. He was knighted in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to the chemical sciences and elected an Honorary Fellow of the Chinese Chemical Society in 2015. In 2016, he received the Lord Lewis Prize for his work on supercritical fluids and science policy in the EU and globally, and was elected Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (FAAAS) and Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering (FREng). In 2019, he was awarded the Royal Society of London Michael Faraday Prize for science communication and the Longstaff Prize for his contributions to green chemistry and the creation of Periodic Videos. In 2023, he was elected a Foreign Academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in the chemistry division. A tram in Nottingham's tram network was named after him in 2021. He has a daughter, Ellen Poliakoff, who is a psychology lecturer at the University of Manchester, and a son, Simon Poliakoff, who is a physics teacher at The Priory School Hitchin. In 2010, Poliakoff produced a web eulogy for his close friend Tony Judt.
